title: Two books for one camp
hook: a Persian poet and a Roman emperor, read side by side, each in his own world

segments.voice: Yesterday, askesis: a whole camp of practice in one small routine. Your line was I can do this. Today, a new camp.

Two men who could never have met. One is a Roman emperor in a cold army camp by the Danube river, around the year 170, writing at night by lamplight in a private notebook, reminding himself how to be a decent person. The other is a Muslim scholar in the city of Konya, in what is now Turkey, a thousand years later, reciting long poems full of stories while a student writes them down. One speaks Greek, one Persian. One leans on reason, the other on longing for God. For the next seventy-five days, you'll read them side by side.
screen: `AN EMPEROR BY THE DANUBE.` → `A POET IN KONYA.` → `TWO BOOKS FOR ONE CAMP.`

segments.voice: The first book is the Meditations of Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome. You've already met him: the view from above, the morning preview. He wrote it in Greek, not Latin, in twelve short books, and most scholars think he never meant anyone else to read it. The oldest manuscripts give it a title that means simply to himself; the name Meditations was added much later. So you're reading someone's private notes: "Begin the morning by saying to thyself," one famous entry starts, and then lists the difficult people he expects to meet. The second book is the Masnavi of Jalal al-Din Rumi. It's enormous, about twenty-five thousand couplets in six books, in Persian, full of stories: merchants, parrots, kings, lovers, a reed flute. Rumi was a Muslim scholar and a teacher of Islamic law, steeped in the Qur'an, and the Masnavi is soaked in it. Some Persian speakers have called it the Qur'an in Persian, a phrase that tells you how deeply it's loved. Here's how this camp works. You'll read in paraphrase and in careful older translations, one story or one passage at a time. Each man stays in his own world. Marcus is a Stoic who trusts reason and duty. Rumi is a Muslim mystic who speaks of longing for God. I won't pretend they're saying the same thing, and I won't make one of them the winner. Just listen to each, and notice what happens in you when two different voices sit side by side.
screen: `TO HIMSELF: THE MEDITATIONS.` · `THE MASNAVI: SIX BOOKS OF STORIES.` · `EACH IN HIS OWN WORLD.` · `LISTEN TO EACH, NO WINNER.` · then, large: `TWO VOICES.`

segments.voice: If you can, pick up two real books, any two, one in each hand; if not, rest your hands on your knees, palms up, and imagine them. Feel the weight of each: different sizes, different worlds. Don't choose between them; just hold both, and let your breath move between your hands.
Masnavi, Rumi's long Persian poem of about twenty-five thousand couplets, read side by side with Marcus's notebook this camp. Today's word.
Your line: two voices. Each one stays in its own world. Tomorrow, a boy leaves the east.

screen: `DAY 157 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A BOY LEAVES THE EAST.`

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often read a short entry each morning, and readers of Rumi's Masnavi traditionally read it slowly, story by story, sometimes in study circles, especially in Turkey, Iran and South Asia.

original.note: Greek, ta eis heauton: to himself, the title in the oldest manuscripts of the Meditations.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Meditations is a self-help book an emperor wrote for us.
what it means: private notes, never meant for readers, now read beside a very different book.
what a scholar hears: the manuscript title ta eis heauton; the Masnavi-yi Ma'navi, which Jami is often said to have called 'the Qur'an in Persian'.

sources.quoted: Begin the morning by saying to thyself

notes: Meditations 2.1, Long 1862: 'Begin the morning by saying to thyself...' confirm wording.
Marcus wrote at least part of the Meditations on campaign (Book 1 ends 'among the Quadi at the Granua'; Book 2 'at Carnuntum'); 'around the year 170' by the Danube is approximate.

Masnavi: about 25,000 to 26,000 couplets in six books; confirm. The phrase 'the Qur'an in Persian' is traditionally attributed to Jami; hedged as 'some Persian speakers have called it'. Islam Keeper to confirm framing.
'Trusts reason' vs. 'love of God' is a simplified contrast, stated without ranking; a reviewer may want to soften it.
Tomorrow's story (Rumi's birth and journey west) is not taught today.

Reviewer fix: 'almost certainly never meant anyone to read it' softened to 'most scholars think'; the private-notebook reading is the majority view but a minority argue for some intended audience. Hook contrast changed from 'trusts reason / love of God' to 'leans on reason / longing for God', since Marcus also writes of the gods and providence.
Hook says Rumi lived 'a thousand years later'; the gap is roughly 1,050 to 1,100 years. Acceptable as a round figure.
